title: Gravity sets an upper limit on the size of terrestrial animals

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Gravity sets an upper limit on the size of terrestrial animals

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because the strength of muscles and the crushing resistance of bones vary as their cross-section (the square of linear size) while body weight varies as the cube, there is a definite upper limit to the size of an animal living under gravity; the elephant, with disproportionately thick limb bones and reduced agility, is already near it.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: strength \propto L^2, W \propto L^3 \Rightarrow strength/W \propto L^{-1}, so L is bounded above under gravity

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But in a terrestrial animal the weight which tends to crush its limbs or which its muscles have to move, varies as the cube of its linear dimensions; and so, to the possible magnitude of an animal, living under the direct action of gravity, there is a definite limit set.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter II, “On Magnitude”; topic “Strength, weight and size limits”. Scope: terrestrial animals, especially large mammals

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: strength \propto L^2, W \propto L^3 \Rightarrow strength/W \propto L^{-1}, so L is bounded above under gravity

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch02-03: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing morphology and trait data can test scaling and estimate mechanical margins across many terrestrial mammals. They cannot cleanly establish a definite universal maximum, because lineages alter posture and structure and because extinct giants require incomplete fossil reconstructions.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate limb-bone cross-sectional area, body mass, muscle area and locomotor performance across terrestrial species, test the predicted square-cube scaling, and calculate safety factors and failure thresholds. Departure from the proposed scaling or viable taxa beyond the predicted bound would count against the mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No observed fauna samples the counterfactual sizes near a universal failure limit.

Posture, gait, bone geometry and material properties confound simple square-cube scaling.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data existence: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.6
operationalizability: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The square-cube contrast is a definite prediction about bone allometry and maximum terrestrial mass, and both masses and scannable limb bones exist. They are not one joint dataset, mammal coverage is better than the full scope of terrestrial animals, and a thick elephant limb does not show that bone stress, rather than some other constraint, sets the ceiling. The analysis is feasible for a subset and takes more than a routine few weeks if scans must be measured and matched.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate compressive stress from body mass and limb-bone cross-section under gravity. The claim is supported if safety factor falls with size unless bones thicken faster than isometry, and if the largest land mammals sit near a practical ceiling; it is weakened if elephants retain small-mammal safety factors or if much larger terrestrial animals have ordinary limb proportions.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Safety factors need posture and duty factor, which mass and diameter do not contain.

Bone meshes and body-mass tables are not linked individual by individual.

Food, heat, and life history can limit size even when bone stress does not.

operationalizability: 0.7
